title: FAITH WILL BECOME SIGHT. HOPE WILL BE FULFILLED. BUT LOVE WILL NEVER END.
paragraphs: FAITH WILL BECOME SIGHT. HOPE WILL BE FULFILLED. BUT LOVE WILL NEVER END.
Why Did God Call Love the Greatest? The Answer Will Confront the Way You Believe, the Way You Treat People, and What You Think It Really Means to Follow Jesus.
What if you could believe every promise in the Bible, understand its deepest mysteries, give away everything you own, and still miss the very heart of God?
Not because you didn't pray enough.
Not because you didn't attend church.
Not because you didn't know enough Scripture.
But because somewhere along the way, you learned how to practice Christianity without learning how to love.
That possibility should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Especially those of us who have been Christians for years.
Because there is something frightening about being able to quote the words of Jesus while slowly becoming unlike Him.
You can defend the truth and still destroy someone with your tongue.
You can sing about grace and still refuse to extend forgiveness.
You can post Bible verses every morning and make the people living under your roof feel unwanted every evening.
You can be admired by an entire congregation while the people who know you best are quietly wounded by the way you treat them.
And then, in the middle of one of the most extraordinary chapters ever written about the Christian life, the apostle Paul says something that should stop us in our tracks.
“And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.” — 1 Corinthians 13:13, KJV
That word charity in the King James Version translates the Greek word ἀγάπη (agapē), commonly rendered love in modern English translations.
Faith.
Hope.
Love.
Three extraordinary gifts.
Three realities at the center of Christian existence.
But one is called the greatest.
And the question is not merely why love ranks above the other two.
The deeper question is this:
What does God see in love that we so often fail to see?
Because when you finally understand Paul's answer, you may discover that the most important evidence of your spiritual maturity is not how much Scripture you can explain.
It is how much of Christ's love is becoming visible in your life.
And that changes everything.
Paul did not write 1 Corinthians 13 to decorate wedding invitations.
He wrote it to a church that was spiritually gifted but deeply divided.
The Corinthian believers had knowledge, eloquence, spiritual gifts, and strong opinions. Yet jealousy, rivalry, pride, and disorder were tearing at their fellowship.
Some were boasting about their spiritual abilities.
Others were treating fellow believers as less important.
Even their gatherings around the Lord's Supper exposed divisions between the wealthy and the poor.
Imagine that.
A congregation could celebrate the sacrifice of Christ while humiliating people for whom Christ had died.
They had extraordinary spiritual activity.
But their relationships were telling another story.
So Paul confronted them with a truth that remains devastatingly relevant.
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.” — 1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
He goes further.

“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.” — 1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Read that again.
Not I am less impressive.
Not I need a little improvement.
“I am nothing.”
Paul is not saying spiritual gifts are worthless or that faith is unimportant. He is saying that gifts, knowledge, and even extraordinary acts of religious devotion cannot substitute for love.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes we measure our spiritual lives by what people can see.
The ministry we lead.
The verses we memorize.
The arguments we win.
The sacrifices we make.
But God also sees what happens when nobody is applauding.
He sees how we respond when someone disappoints us.
He sees the words we choose when we are angry.
He sees whether we show mercy to people who cannot repay us.
He sees the difference between serving others out of love and serving others because we need to feel important.
And perhaps the hardest truth is this:
A person can become very skilled at appearing spiritual while remaining painfully immature in love.
That is not an accusation against everyone who serves in ministry.
It is a warning to every human heart.
Mine included.
Because none of us is beyond the temptation to make our Christian life about ourselves.
But why is love the greatest?
To understand Paul's statement, we must look carefully at the words he actually used.
In the Greek text of 1 Corinthians 13:13, Paul writes:
Transliterated:
Nyni de menei pistis, elpis, agapē, ta tria tauta; meizōn de toutōn hē agapē.
A close English rendering is:
“And now remain faith, hope, love, these three; but the greatest of these is love.”
Three Greek words deserve our attention.
Πίστις (pistis) means faith, trust, or faithfulness, depending on context. Here it points to the believer's trusting response to God.
Ἐλπίς (elpis) means hope, not mere wishful thinking, but confident expectation grounded in God's promises.
Ἀγάπη (agapē) means love. In this chapter, Paul describes love through patient, kind, humble, truthful, enduring action.
It is important not to exaggerate the Greek.
The word agapē does not automatically mean divine or unconditional love in every ancient Greek sentence. Its meaning is shaped by context.
But in Paul's teaching, this love is profoundly shaped by the character of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
And then comes the word that answers our question.
Μείζων (meizōn).
Greater.
Paul does not say that faith is unnecessary.
He does not say hope is inferior in the sense of being unworthy.
He says that among these three enduring Christian realities, love has the greatest place.
Why?
Because love is not simply one Christian virtue among many.
Love expresses the very character of the God in whom our faith rests and toward whom our hope reaches.
The apostle John writes:
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say that love is God, as though every feeling called love must therefore be holy.
It says God is love.
His character defines what true love is.
And Scripture immediately shows us what that love looks like.
“In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him.” — 1 John 4:9, KJV
Love is not merely something God commands.
It is something He has revealed through the giving of His Son.
And this brings us to a truth so beautiful that it deserves to be considered slowly.
Faith trusts God.
Hope awaits what God has promised.
Love reflects who God is.
Faith reaches toward Him in dependence.
Hope looks toward His coming fulfillment.
Love flows from His character into the way we treat one another.
And that is why love cannot be reduced to a sentimental feeling.
It is far too holy for that.
Think about the person who has hurt you.
The one whose name still makes your chest tighten.
The one who apologized but never seemed to understand the damage.
Or perhaps the one who never apologized at all.
You may have learned to smile again.
You may have learned to function.
But somewhere inside, there is still a conversation you replay, an injustice you remember, a wound that has not fully healed.
And when you hear the command to love, something inside you resists.
Because love sounds dangerous.
Love sounds like letting them win.
Love sounds like pretending nothing happened.
But biblical love is not denial.
It does not call evil good.
It does not demand that victims remain in unsafe relationships.
It does not eliminate accountability or automatically restore broken trust.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13:6 that love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.”
Real love does not bury truth to preserve appearances.
It brings truth and grace together.
Sometimes love means forgiving without taking revenge.
Sometimes love means speaking a difficult truth.
Sometimes love means setting a necessary boundary.
Sometimes love means protecting someone who cannot protect themselves.
And sometimes love means admitting, through tears, that you were the one who caused the wound.
That last one is especially difficult.
Because it is easier to ask God to heal what others did to us than to ask Him to expose what we have done to others.
But grace does not only comfort the wounded.
It also calls the guilty to repentance.
And Jesus is merciful enough to do both.
Now consider another question.
What happens to faith and hope when Christ returns?
Paul has already given us an important clue earlier in the chapter.
“For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.” — 1 Corinthians 13:12, KJV
In Paul's day, a mirror was generally made of polished metal. Its reflection was less clear than the mirrors we know today.
Paul uses that image to describe the limitations of our present understanding.
We know truly, but not completely.
We see something of God's glory, but not yet with the clarity of the promised consummation.
Our spiritual gifts and present knowledge belong to an age in which we still await fullness.
But the day is coming when Christ will bring His people into the fullness of His promised presence.
Romans 8:24 says:
“For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?”
And 2 Corinthians 5:7 tells us:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
These passages help explain why Christians have often understood love's greatness in relation to eternity.
Faith presently trusts what is not yet seen.
Hope presently awaits what is not yet fully received.
When God's promises are fulfilled, the conditions under which we now exercise faith and hope will be transformed.
We will no longer wait for Christ's return after He has returned.
We will no longer long for the final redemption as though it were still future after God has brought it to completion.
This does not mean that trust in God becomes worthless or that joyful confidence disappears in eternity.
Nor should we claim that Paul explicitly says faith and hope will cease to exist.
In fact, he says these three remain.
His central contrast in the chapter is between what is partial and temporary and what is enduring.
But love is explicitly described in verse 8 as never failing.
“Charity never faileth.”
The Greek expression is:
“Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε πίπτει.”
Hē agapē oudepote piptei.
In context, it communicates that love never falls away or comes to an end, in contrast with gifts that will cease or pass away.
Love belongs to the life of God's people now, and it will not be discarded when perfection comes.
Imagine that for a moment.
No more sin poisoning relationships.
No more jealousy hiding behind congratulations.
No more pride demanding recognition.
No more bitterness turning yesterday's wounds into tomorrow's cruelty.
No more love weakened by selfishness.
No more need to wonder whether you are truly welcomed into the presence of the Savior who redeemed you.
The final fulfillment of God's promises will not make love obsolete.
It will bring His people into the fullness of love.
And this is one reason love is so astonishingly great.
Love is not merely preparation for eternity. Love belongs to eternity.
But there is another reason.
And this one leads us directly to the cross.
Because if you want to understand what Christian love truly is, do not begin with a romantic song.
Do not begin with a motivational quotation.
Do not even begin with the most generous person you have ever met.
Begin at Calvary.
Begin with a Savior who had every right to judge sinners and yet willingly gave Himself to save them.
Begin with the One who was betrayed, mocked, rejected, scourged, and crucified.
Begin with Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became spiritually impressive.
Not after we proved ourselves deserving.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And this is where the Gospel becomes scandalous to human pride.
Because we naturally want grace to be a reward for improvement.
We want God to love us because we finally became lovable.
We want our repentance, obedience, and religious activity to establish our worthiness.
But the Gospel announces something far more humbling.
We could not save ourselves.
Our sin was real.
Our guilt was real.
God's holiness was not negotiable.
And yet, out of His extraordinary love, God sent His Son.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience, died for our sins, and rose again.
Salvation is not purchased by our religious performance.
It is received by grace through faith in Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Do you see the beauty?
Faith is essential because it is through faith that we receive God's saving grace.
Hope is precious because God's promises give us confidence beyond suffering and death.
And love is greatest because it is the divine love revealed in Christ that stands at the very heart of our redemption and becomes the pattern of our transformed lives.
The cross does not make faith unnecessary.
The resurrection does not make hope unnecessary.
The Gospel gives faith its foundation, hope its certainty, and love its clearest revelation.
And perhaps you need to hear this today.
You may have made a terrible mess of your life.
You may be carrying a past that still makes you ashamed.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you destroyed a relationship through selfishness.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind religious language because you are terrified of admitting how far you have wandered.
Maybe you still attend church.
Still worship.
Still smile when someone asks how you are doing.
But deep down, you know there are things you need to bring into the light.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not call you to pretend your sin is harmless.
He calls you to repent.
And He does not call you to repent because His mercy is too small for your failure.
He calls you because His mercy is greater than your excuses, and His grace is powerful enough to change your life.
You do not have to defend what Christ came to forgive.
You do not have to keep wearing a mask to impress people who also need mercy.
You can come into the light.
You can confess.
You can turn away from sin.
You can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Your past may explain some of your scars, but it does not have the authority to overrule the redemption found in Jesus Christ.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not that every consequence disappears.
Not that every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not that repentance erases the need to make things right.
But that the grace of Christ can change the direction of a human life.
The liar can learn to walk in truth.
The proud can learn humility.
The bitter can learn forgiveness.
The selfish can learn generosity.
The spiritually exhausted can find renewed strength in the Lord.
The sinner can receive mercy.
And the person who once lived for self can begin living for Christ.
That is not cosmetic improvement.
That is transformation.
But let us return to Paul's words.
Because there is something in 1 Corinthians 13 that should make us examine not only what we believe but how we live.
“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.” — 1 Corinthians 13:4, KJV
Love is patient.
Love is kind.
Love does not envy.
Love does not boast.
Love is not arrogant.
Now imagine replacing the word love with your own name.
Can you say those things truthfully?
Are you patient with your family?
Are you kind when you are tired?
Can you celebrate another person's blessing without secretly resenting it?
Can you apologize without adding a long explanation about why you were technically justified?
Can you listen without preparing your defense?
Can you correct someone without humiliating them?
Can you disagree without becoming cruel?
Can you serve without needing everyone to know?
These questions reach into places where religious appearances cannot protect us.
And perhaps that is why we sometimes prefer debates about theology over obedience to the theology we already know.
It can feel easier to explain the Greek word for love than to practice patience with someone who irritates us.
Easier to defend biblical marriage than to speak tenderly to our spouse.
Easier to preach about forgiveness than to release our desire for revenge.
Easier to condemn the sins of strangers than to confess the pride in our own hearts.
But Jesus never separated love from obedience.
He said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” — John 14:15, KJV
And He also said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — John 13:35, KJV
Not by the size of our platforms.
Not by the beauty of our church buildings.
Not by the number of arguments we win online.
But by our love for one another.
This does not mean doctrine is unimportant.
It means sound doctrine should lead us toward the character of Christ.
Truth and love are not enemies.
Biblical love rejoices in truth.
And biblical truth should never become an excuse for loveless cruelty.
The apostle Paul brings them together in Ephesians 4:15 when he speaks of “speaking the truth in love.”
A church without truth can lose its faithfulness to Christ.
A church that speaks truth without love can betray the character of the Christ it proclaims.
We need both.
And perhaps our world needs to see that union more desperately than ever.
Think about how quickly people are condemned online.
How easily Christians mock those with whom they disagree.
How readily believers share outrage while overlooking the person quietly struggling in front of them.
There are people who no longer want to enter a church because the Christians they encountered seemed more interested in winning than in loving.
Of course, the failures of Christians do not invalidate the truth of Christ.
But they should humble those of us who bear His name.
We cannot change every person who has been hurt by religion.
We cannot repair every wrong committed by someone claiming to represent Jesus.
But we can repent where we have contributed to the damage.
We can refuse to excuse cruelty as boldness.
We can speak truth with gentleness.
We can become people whose lives make the Gospel more visible, not less.
And that brings us to something we must never forget.
Love is not the price we pay to earn salvation. Love is the fruit that should grow from a life being transformed by God's grace.
Galatians 5:22 begins its description of the fruit of the Spirit with love.
And 1 John 4:19 says:
“We love him, because he first loved us.”
There is the order.
God loved us first.
His grace awakens our response.
His Spirit transforms us.
And we learn to love because we have been loved.
We do not become Christians by successfully imitating God's love.
We are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ, and then His grace begins to reshape how we live.
That distinction matters.
Because some of you are reading this and feeling convicted.
You know you have not been patient.
You know your words have wounded people.
You know there are relationships in which you have been stubborn, proud, or unforgiving.
And conviction can be painful.
But do not confuse the Holy Spirit's call to repentance with the lie that you are beyond God's mercy.
The purpose of godly conviction is not to drive you into hopelessness.
It is to bring you back to the truth.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ receives those who come to Him in faith.
And the same grace that forgives also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
You may need to apologize today.
Not tomorrow.
Not when the other person finally admits everything they did wrong.
Today.
You may need to tell your child, “I was wrong to speak to you that way.”
You may need to tell your spouse, “I've been so busy defending myself that I stopped listening to your pain.”
You may need to tell a friend, “I should have been there for you.”
You may need to tell God, “Lord, I've been using Your name while neglecting Your heart.”
And perhaps you need to pray the words of Psalm 51:10:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
Not a more impressive image.
Not a larger audience.
Not a reputation for being the strongest Christian in the room.
A clean heart.
A renewed spirit.
A life increasingly shaped by Jesus.
Because one day, the applause will fade.
The social media posts will disappear into forgotten timelines.
The arguments that consumed our energy will no longer seem so important.
The titles we held will not be the measure of our eternal worth.
And the question will not be whether we managed to impress the world with our spirituality.
What will matter is whether we truly belonged to Christ.
And those who belong to Him are called to love as He loved.
That does not mean every genuine believer loves perfectly.
None of us does.
We still struggle.
We still fail.
We still need repentance and grace.
But the direction of a life transformed by Christ is toward love, not away from it.
Toward humility.
Toward mercy.
Toward holiness.
Toward truth.
Toward obedience.
Toward the character of the Savior.
This is why 1 Corinthians 13 should never become merely a beautiful passage we read at weddings.
It should become a mirror before which we examine our lives.
And a window through which we behold the beauty of Jesus.
Because He is the perfect embodiment of the love Paul describes.
He was patient with struggling disciples.
He showed compassion to the outcast.
He spoke truth to the proud.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He did not rejoice in evil.
He endured suffering in obedience to the Father.
He loved not merely in words but in sacrificial action.
And on the cross, He revealed a love no human achievement could equal.
That love does not merely inspire us.
Through the Gospel, it saves and transforms us.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a test of how religious you sound.
Not as an invitation to perform spirituality in public.
But as an opportunity to be honest before God.
Where is Jesus teaching you to love more deeply right now?
Is it in your marriage?
Your relationship with your parents?
Your treatment of your children?
Your response to someone who betrayed you?
Your attitude toward people who disagree with you?
Or is it in the hidden place where you are finally learning to receive the love of God instead of trying to earn it?
You can simply write “Lord, teach me to love like Jesus.”
Or share a testimony about how Christ has been changing your heart.
You do not have to reveal private wounds or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest words may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone in the journey of repentance, healing, and growth.
And if you know someone who has been wounded by loveless religion, consider sharing this article with them.
Not to accuse them.
Not to pressure them.
But to remind them that the failures of human beings do not define the heart of Jesus Christ.
Because this ministry is not meant to be another place where people simply consume religious content and move on.
Our desire is to help people grow deeper in the Word of God, understand the Gospel faithfully, confront sin honestly, receive grace humbly, and follow Jesus more closely.
These resources are intended to help believers nourish their faith, deepen their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their walk with Christ, and share biblical truth with others.
And I want to speak to those of you who have been blessed by this ministry.
Like other voluntary offerings made for the work of ministry, it can be given with gratitude to God and a desire to serve others.
But I also want to be biblically careful here.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to prove your love for Jesus.
But willing generosity, according to your ability and conviction, for a ministry you believe is faithfully serving Christ.
If you are already supporting your local church and other ministries, we honor that commitment.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
Pray for this ministry.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone who is hurting.
Help someone understand the Word of God.
Love your family.
Serve your local church.
Show compassion to the forgotten.
Because the goal has never been to build a community that merely admires Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people to the Savior who alone can save them.
And that brings us back to where we began.
Faith.
Hope.
Love.
Three extraordinary realities.
Faith holds to the promises of God even when the road is dark.
Hope keeps looking toward Christ even when suffering seems endless.
And love teaches us to live in a way that reflects the Savior we trust and the glorious future we await.
Perhaps your faith feels weak today.
Perhaps hope seems distant.
Perhaps you are discovering just how difficult it is to love someone who has wounded you.
Remember this.
The answer is not to manufacture stronger feelings through sheer determination.
The answer is to return to Jesus Christ.
Look again at His cross.
Remember His resurrection.
Receive His Word.
Depend upon His Spirit.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Make peace where it is right and possible.
Set wise boundaries where necessary.
And ask the Lord to make your life increasingly reflect His love.
Because love is not a substitute for faith.
Love is not a substitute for hope.
And love is certainly not a substitute for the saving work of Jesus.
But the love of God revealed in Christ gives us the clearest picture of what redeemed humanity is being transformed to become.
One day, we will see more clearly than we see now.
One day, God's promises will reach their appointed fulfillment.
One day, the people of Christ will dwell with Him in a creation where sin and death no longer have dominion.
And love will not be left behind.
The love that brought the Son of God into the world.
The love revealed at the cross.
The love poured into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit.
The love that teaches us to forgive, serve, repent, and persevere.
That love will never become obsolete.
And until that glorious day, may we never be content merely to talk about it.
May we live it.
May our homes experience it.
May our churches demonstrate it.
May our enemies encounter its patience and truth.
May the wounded discover its compassion.
May the lost hear through our words and see through our lives the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And when our own love fails, may we return again and again to the One whose love never does.
Because the greatest Christian life is not the one that makes the most noise.
It is the one increasingly surrendered to the Savior whose love changes everything.
When everything you once used to prove your faith has faded from view, may the people you touched still remember something of the love of Jesus in you.
